extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry/literary style
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for judging or composing poetry, with emphasis on natural diction, imaginative origin, congruence of thought and language, and principles of fair criticism. The guidance is aimed at readers studying poetic aesthetics and critical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination's internal rules (no external prescription)
rubrics_metrics.description: Could a rule be given from without, poetry would cease to be poetry ... The rules of the imagination are themselves the very powers of growth and production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry must arise from the internal laws of imagination rather than imposed external rules. Attempts to prescribe a fixed set of external rules risk turning poetry into a mechanical art. Evaluate whether language and form feel organically produced by the poet's imaginative powers rather than pasted-on technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality over superficial form
rubrics_metrics.description: The words...present only the outlines and external appearance of the fruit. A deceptive counterfeit of the superficial form and colours may be elaborated; but the marble peach feels cold and heavy, and children only put it to their mouths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that convey living feeling and inward truth rather than convincing surface ornament. Distinguish genuine emotional/ideational substance from mere decorative verbal effects; examples of genuine feeling given (e.g., Donne's apostrophe to the Sun) serve as positive models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness / accordance with actual language
rubrics_metrics.description: He meant to confine his theory of style...to a close accordance with the actual language of men ... the language of nature and of good sense, even in its humblest and least ornamented forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether diction suits the subject and approximates natural speech where appropriate (especially for humble or rustic subjects). Overly artificial phrasing that departs from conversational usage, without compensating poetic justification, is a defect. Examples: Wordsworth's advocacy for language resembling ordinary speech; Chaucer and Herbert as models of natural yet dignified diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of pseudo-poesy and affected extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude from the honours...the madness prepense of pseudo-poesy, or the startling hysteric of weakness over-exerting itself, which bursts on the unprepared reader in sundry odes and apostrophes to abstract terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag works that rely on extravagant, affected devices (e.g., Odes to Jealousy, Hope, Oblivion) where the effect is more theatrical than sincere. Such hysteric, contrived passion or apostrophizing of abstractions is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apt expression: marry thought to metre and rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: The talent that is required...is the talent to seek only the apt expression of the thought, and yet to find at the same time with it the rhyme and the metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value poets who express thought as one would wish to speak while simultaneously securing musical form. Judge whether rhyme and metre feel natural outcomes of expression rather than constraints forcing awkward diction (Garve's ideal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence between thought and language
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic fault of our elder poets is the reverse of that which distinguishes too many of our more recent versifiers; the one conveying the most fantastic thoughts in the most correct and natural language, the other in the most fantastic language conveying the most trivial thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the match between the subject-matter's seriousness or novelty and the language used. Avoid mismatch: grandiose language for trivial content, or trivial phrasing for weighty ideas. Aim for harmony between concept and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of juxtaposition and surprise as a controlled device
rubrics_metrics.description: Their operation consists in the excitement of surprise by the juxtaposition and apparent reconciliation of widely different or incompatible things...it is therefore a species of wit, a pure work of the will, and implies a leisure and self-possession both of thought and of feeling, incompatible with the steady fervour of a mind possessed and filled with the grandeur of its subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat striking metaphors and bold juxtapositions as an intentional wit that requires composure; they are appropriate when the poem's voice can sustain deliberate, skillful artifice, but are unsuitable when the work aims for spontaneous fervour or heartfelt passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sober majesty and clarity in lofty sense
rubrics_metrics.description: In the sober majesty of lofty sense...it appeared to them to approach more nearly than any other poetry they had heard to the style of our Bible in the prophetic books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For elevated themes, prefer language that balances grandeur with clarity and gravity rather than chaotic rhetorical excess. Translations or imitations that preserve impressive, measured movement and clear connections are models (example: proper treatment of Pindaric material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate register, prosody, and historical pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the reader adopt the pronunciation of the poet and of the court at which he lived, both with respect to the final e and to the accentuation of the last syllable...what could we hear more natural...than the following stanzas from Chaucer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical and prosodic appropriateness: pronunciation, accent, and metrical practices can affect perceived naturalness. Evaluations should account for period-appropriate diction and metre rather than imposing modern norms blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognisable individual style (distinctive diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A similar peculiarity...attends Mr. Wordsworth's style, whenever he speaks in his own person...it cannot be imitated without being at once recognised as originating in Mr. Wordsworth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value a distinct, individual voice that consistently recurs across a poet's work. Distinctiveness is an aesthetic merit when it enhances meaning and feeling, though rigidly enforcing one 'theory' of style may erase valuable idiosyncrasies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammatical and syntactic choice as expressive tool
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a peculiarity—the frequent use of the disjunctive (i.e. the omission of the active particle before the last of several words)...and not less in the struction of words by apposition...In short, grammatic construction is not unfrequently peculiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether unusual syntax, omission, apposition, or other grammatical choices serve expressive ends. Such departures from ordinary grammar can be powerful devices if they aid rhythm, emphasis, or voice; they are faults if gratuitous or obscuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish accident from characteristic in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularize the most striking passages to which [canons] are applicable, faithfully noticing the frequent or infrequent recurrence of similar merits or defects, and as faithfully distinguishing what is characteristic from what is accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In criticism, identify whether praised or blamed features are systemic to the poet's work (characteristic) or occasional (accidental). Base judgments on patterns across works, not on isolated lapses or flashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair, philosophical method for criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: I should call that investigation fair and philosophical, in which the critic announces and endeavours to establish the principles, which he holds for the foundation of poetry in general, with the specification of these in their application to the different classes of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should state their premises and canons, apply them consistently to examples, make rational deductions, and present conclusions transparently. This aids readers and authors to understand, accept, or dispute the judgement on rational grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and tone of criticism: avoid personal invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Every censure...respecting a publication which the critic, with the criticized work before him, can make good, is the critic's right. The writer is authorized to reply, but not to complain...as long as no personal allusions are admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censure is legitimate when grounded in the work; avoid ad hominem attacks or dredging up juvenile performances to malign the author. Critics must weigh their words for the intended effect and refrain from gossiping, backbiting, or malignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity and purposefulness of reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme of reviewing those books only which are susceptible and deserving of argumentative criticism...supplying the vacant place of the trash or mediocrity wisely left to sink into oblivion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and journals should focus critical effort on works that merit argument and engagement rather than giving space to every mediocre piece. Use reviews to advance thoughtful discussion rather than amplify triviality.
